source.title: The control of tonic pain by active relief learning.

confidence_rationale: A human computational-neuroimaging study that models active relief-seeking explicitly as a reinforcement-learning process with reward-prediction-error signals in dorsal putamen and an associability (uncertainty) signal in pregenual ACC that gates the relief learning rate. This is a near one-to-one structural match for REE's MECH-375 Q_relief term (action-contingent escape credit learned by RL prediction error). Confidence held below 0.8 because the task is tonic-pain relief in humans, not a committed navigational escape, and because it models the relief component in isolation -- it does not contrast relief against a safety/threat-absence predictor, so it speaks to one arm of Q-067's decomposition rather than to the relief-vs-safety discriminator.
failure_signatures: Relief-seeking that is modelled without an RL error term would fail to reproduce the dorsal-putamen prediction-error signature this study reports; a fixed (non-trainable) escape bridge therefore cannot capture the associability-modulated relief dynamics.
The study isolates the relief/active-escape arm and does not include a safety predictor, so it cannot show whether relief alone suffices when a fixed bridge is insufficient.

mapping.source_claim_statement: In two human escape-learning experiments (static and dynamic), active relief-seeking from tonic pain is implemented as a reinforcement-learning process: relief prediction errors are observed in dorsal putamen, and an associability/uncertainty signal in pregenual anterior cingulate cortex both sets the relief learning rate and parametrically modulates the ongoing level of tonic pain.
mapping.ree_translation: This is the biological template for REE's MECH-375 Q_relief successor -- action-contingent escape credit acquired by reinforcement learning. The putamen prediction-error signal corresponds to the trainable relief-credit term REE would add on top of the fixed escape bridge, and the pgACC associability signal corresponds to an uncertainty-gated learning-rate on that term. The finding that relief learning is an active, error-driven, uncertainty-modulated RL process (not a static affordance) supports building Q_relief as a trainable head rather than relying on the fixed first-action-class bridge.
mapping.mapping_caveat: The paper models the relief arm only; it includes no safety/threat-absence predictor and so cannot adjudicate relief-only vs safety-only vs both-required -- it strengthens the case that the relief component is genuinely a learnable RL term but does not show it is the missing piece. Domain is tonic-pain offset in humans, not committed spatial escape.
mapping.source_context: Healthy adult humans; static and dynamic escape-learning tasks under tonic thermal/pressure pain; fMRI + computational RL modelling.

confidence_components.notes: Strong venue and converging behavioural/physiological/imaging evidence with an explicit RL model; mapping is high for the Q_relief arm specifically but does not reach the relief-vs-safety contrast. Human tonic-pain domain transfers only moderately to a committed-escape agent.
